      4         }
      6 print(my_dict)

TypeError: unhashable type: 'dict'

Dictionary Key Restrictions¶

In [69]:
# keys are immutable: tuples are accepted as keys
my_dict = { 
        ( 'courses' , 'English', 'Maths' ): { 'Sarah': 21, 'Bob': 19 } 
        }
print(my_dict)

{('courses', 'English', 'Maths'): {'Sarah': 21, 'Bob': 19}}

Dictionary Methods - A Simple Example¶

In [70]:
# The rooms dictionary
rooms = {
    'Hall': {
        'south': 'Kitchen',
        'item': 'key',},
    'Kitchen': {
        'north': 'Hall',
        'item': 'monster'},
    'Dining Room': {
        'west': 'Hall',
        'item': 'potion'}}
print(f"Initial 'rooms' dictionary: \n{rooms}")

Initial 'rooms' dictionary: 
{'Hall': {'south': 'Kitchen', 'item': 'key'}, 'Kitchen': {'north': 'Hall', 'item': 'monster'}, 'Dining Room': {'west': 'Hall', 'item': 'potion'}}

Dictionary Methods¶

  • D.keys() that returns the keys of a dictionary
  • D.values() that returns the values of a dictionary
In [71]:
# Using D.keys() method
print(f"Keys of the 'rooms' dictionary are rooms.keys(): \n{rooms.keys()}\n")

# Using D.values() method
print(f"Values of the 'rooms' dictionary are rooms.values(): \n{rooms.values()}")

Keys of the 'rooms' dictionary are rooms.keys(): 
dict_keys(['Hall', 'Kitchen', 'Dining Room'])

Values of the 'rooms' dictionary are rooms.values(): 
dict_values([{'south': 'Kitchen', 'item': 'key'}, {'north': 'Hall', 'item': 'monster'}, {'west': 'Hall', 'item': 'potion'}])

Dictionary Methods¶

  • D.items() that returns the key-value pairs of a dictionary
  • D.get(key) that returns the value associated with a key
In [72]:
# Using D.items() method
print(f"Key-value pairs of the 'rooms' dictionary are rooms.items():\n{rooms.items()}\n")

# Using D.get(key) method
print(f"Values associated with the key 'Kitchen' can be retrieved using rooms.get('Kitchen'):\n {rooms.get('Kitchen')}")

Key-value pairs of the 'rooms' dictionary are rooms.items():
dict_items([('Hall', {'south': 'Kitchen', 'item': 'key'}), ('Kitchen', {'north': 'Hall', 'item': 'monster'}), ('Dining Room', {'west': 'Hall', 'item': 'potion'})])

Values associated with the key 'Kitchen' can be retrieved using rooms.get('Kitchen'):
 {'north': 'Hall', 'item': 'monster'}

Dictionary Methods¶

  • D.update(D1) adds the key-value pairs of dictionary D1 to dictionary D
In [73]:
D1 = {
    'Balcony': {
        'east': 'Hall',
        'degree': 60,
        'item': 'chair'}}# Create a dictionary D1
rooms.update(D1) # Update the 'rooms' dictionary with new data
# Display both D1 and the updated 'rooms' dictionary
print(f"D1 = {{'Balcony': {{'east': 'Hall', 'degree': 60, 'item': 'chair'}}}} results in:\n {D1}\n")
print(f"The command rooms.update(D1) updates the 'rooms' dictionary to: \n{rooms}")

D1 = {'Balcony': {'east': 'Hall', 'degree': 60, 'item': 'chair'}} results in:
 {'Balcony': {'east': 'Hall', 'degree': 60, 'item': 'chair'}}

The command rooms.update(D1) updates the 'rooms' dictionary to: 
{'Hall': {'south': 'Kitchen', 'item': 'key'}, 'Kitchen': {'north': 'Hall', 'item': 'monster'}, 'Dining Room': {'west': 'Hall', 'item': 'potion'}, 'Balcony': {'east': 'Hall', 'degree': 60, 'item': 'chair'}}

Retrieving Values from Dictionary Using Keys and Indexing¶

  • To retrieve a value, you can also use Indexing with key
    • D[key]
  • If the key doesn't exist, a KeyError will be raised.
In [74]:
mydic = {'Howard': 'aerospace engineer', 'Leonard': 'physicist', 'Sheldon': 'physicist', 
         'Penny': 'waitress', 'Raj': 'astrophysicist'}
print(f"mydic = {{'Howard': 'aerospace engineer', 'Leonard': 'physicist', 'Sheldon': 'physicist', 'Penny': 'waitress', 'Raj': 'astrophysicist'}}")
print(f"Retrieving value for 'Howard' using mydic['Howard'] results in: {mydic['Howard']}")

mydic = {'Howard': 'aerospace engineer', 'Leonard': 'physicist', 'Sheldon': 'physicist', 'Penny': 'waitress', 'Raj': 'astrophysicist'}
Retrieving value for 'Howard' using mydic['Howard'] results in: aerospace engineer

Comparing Dictionaries with Lists¶

  • Similarities
    1. Both allow for heterogeneous types, which can be nested
    2. Both dictionaries and lists enable for the retrieval
      • of an element via its unique index in case of lists (and strings)
      • of a value via its unique key in case of dictionaries
    3. Both can be modified
      • Lists can be modified via the append() and insert() methods
      • Dictionaries can be modified via the update() method

Python List Methods Exercises¶

Exercise 1: Basic Append
Start with the list [1, 2, 3]. Append the integer 4 to it.

Exercise 2: Insert at Index
Start with the list ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]. Insert the fruit "orange" at index 2.

Exercise 3: Remove Element
Start with the list ["red", "blue", "green"]. Remove the color "red" from it.

Exercise 4: Extend List
Start with two lists: ["cat", "dog"] and ["fish", "bird"]. Extend the first list by adding all the elements from the second list.

Exercise 5: Sort Numbers
Start with the list my_list5 = [9, 3, 6, 1, 7]. Create a new list with the sorted elements of my_list5. Print both lists

Exercise 6: Sort Strings
Start with the list ["Apple", "banana", "Cherry", "apple"]. Sort them in lexicographical order, notice the order of precedence between upper-case and lower-case letters.

Exercise 7: Insert and Remove
Start with the list ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"]. Insert "Sunday" at index 0 and remove "Wednesday".

Exercise 8: Extend and Sort
Start with two lists: [12, 4, 8] and [15, 3, 7]. Extend the first list with the second list and sort the resulting list in ascending order.

Exercise 9: Append, Insert, and Sort
Start with the list [2, 5, 1]. Append the number 10, insert the number 100 at index 2, and modify the list so to be sorted xin ascending order.

Exercise 10: Comprehensive Exercise
Start with the list ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"]. Append the names "David" and "Eve", remove "Bob", insert "Frank" at index 3, extend the list with another list ["Grace", "Hannah"], and sort the final list in lexicographical order.

Exercise 11: Advanced List Manipulation

  1. Start with the list my_list11 = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "apple", "banana", "apple"].
  2. Use sort() and observe what happens when you have the same element at different positions.
  3. Use insert() to add "orange" at index 3. Observe how the elements shift. Is the new element where you were expecting it?
  4. Extend my_list11 with the list [1, 2, 3] using the operator + and print the result. Then see if my_list has changed. Do the same using the extend() method
  5. Use my_list11.append([4, 5, 6]) and observe how it differs from my_list11.extend([4, 5, 6]).
  6. Use my_list11.append("grape") and then my_list11.remove("grape"). Observe that the last element is removed.
  7. redefine my_list11 = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "apple", "banana", "apple"]. Use my_list11.append(my_list11) and observe what happens. Try to extract the first element from the last element of the list. Now just extract the last element from my_list11. What do you think is happening?
  8. Use my_list11.sort(reverse=True) to sort the list in descending order.
  9. Use my_list11.pop() to remove the last element from the list and observe the returned value.

Exercise: Loops Using Control Flow and Indexing¶

  1. Given the list of debts amount debt_list = [2000, 30000, 4000, 50000, 6000], write a loop that prints the outstanding debt voices of a company. Write an informative fstring to explain what is printed.

  2. Write another loop that computes and prints the interest cost of each debt entry. The interest rate applied is of the 10% if the debt is below 15000 and 5% if the debt is greater or equal to 15000. Write an informative fstring to explain what is printed. Hint: use the if and elif operators.

  3. Write another loop that that prints: the original debt, the debt+interests and the index of the debt voice. Write an informative fstring to explain what is printed. Hint: you will need to use the range() and len() functions or the enumerate() one.

  4. Augment the previous loop by storing the total debt (including interests) in a new list called debt_list_plusInt. Print the result with an informative fstring. Hint: you can either pre-allocate a list of the expected length or use append.

  5. Finally, modify the previous loop to store the total debt (including interests) in place of the debt_list entries. Print the result with an informative fstring.

Exercise: Analyzing Product Sales¶

You have three lists:

- `products`: A list of product names.
- `sales`: A list of the number of units sold for each product.
- `prices`: A list of the price per unit for each product.


products = ['Apple_Laptop', 'Apple_Mobile', 'Apple_Tablet', 'Samsung_Laptop', 'Samsung_Mobile', 'Samsung_Tablet', 'Sony_Laptop', 'Sony_Mobile', 'Sony_Tablet', 'Dell_Laptop', 'Dell_Mobile', 'Dell_Tablet', 'HP_Laptop', 'HP_Mobile', 'HP_Tablet', 'Nokia_Laptop', 'Nokia_Mobile', 'Nokia_Tablet', 'Asus_Laptop', 'Asus_Mobile', 'Asus_Tablet', 'Acer_Laptop', 'Acer_Mobile', 'Acer_Tablet', 'LG_Laptop', 'LG_Mobile', 'LG_Tablet', 'Lenovo_Laptop', 'Lenovo_Mobile', 'Lenovo_Tablet']
sales = [70, 76, 185, 209, 227, 160, 118, 250, 217, 255, 253, 57, 67, 184, 77, 184, 204, 253, 163, 184, 85, 289, 297, 201, 188, 232, 138, 138, 183, 111]
prices = [1124, 1450, 303, 413, 575, 1438, 360, 400, 380, 596, 1400, 347, 476, 1380, 428, 448, 1446, 977, 1118, 667, 1042, 449, 1199, 1321, 605, 1239, 375, 322, 540, 727]

Given three lists:

  • products: A list of product names.
  • sales: A list of the number of units sold for each product.
  • prices: A list of the price per unit for each product.

1. Product Revenue Display:

  • Loop through the products, sales, and prices.
  • For each product, compute its total revenue (sales * price).
  • Print an f-string that details the product's name and its total revenue.

2. Revenue Analysis:

  • Using the same loop from step 1, store the computed revenues for each product in a new list.

    a. Total Revenue: Calculate and print the overall total revenue from all products.

    b. Top 5 Performers: Calculate the combined revenue of the top 5 products with the highest revenues.

    c. Mid-tier Performers: Calculate the combined revenue of products ranked 20th to 30th in terms of revenue.

    d. Bottom 20 Performers: Calculate the combined revenue of the 20 products with the lowest revenues.

    e. Revenue Extremes: Identify and print the names of the products with the absolute lowest and highest revenues.

    f. Price Extremes: Identify and print the names of the products with the absolute lowest and highest prices and identify their revenues.

    g. Revenue Percentages: For the revenues computed in sub-tasks a to f, calculate and print their percentages relative to the overall total revenue.

3. Use of zip Function:

  • If you haven't used the zip function in the previous steps, modify your code to utilize it for iterating through the products, sales, and prices simultaneously.
